item.title: Hydrodynamic flow in the gut hinders the fixation of beneficial mutants but accelerates their invasion
item.description: arXiv:2611.00134v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gut bacteria experience a spatially structured environment with hydrodynamic flow. Using a branching-process approach, we show that beneficial mutants arising randomly upon division have a reduced fixation probability compared to the well-mixed case. The suppression factor is set by the spatial heterogeneity of mutant fate across the gut. In contrast, the invasion of mutant lineages that avoid early stochastic extinction is accelerated in the gut compared to a matched well-mixed case. Stronger advective flow decreases fixation probabilities while accelerating mutant invasion.
item.dc:creator: Arthur Alexandre, Claude Loverdo, Anne-Florence Bitbol

item.title: How timing and mode of selection shape ancestral genetic contributions
item.description: arXiv:2611.00161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examine a population that evolves according to a biparental Moran model with two distinct types of individuals. Each individual's type is determined by the allele they carry at one biallelic locus, which is transmitted in a Mendelian way. This type influences the individual's mating preferences. We investigate two specific mating patterns: (i) where the type determines the level of attractiveness, and (ii) where the type dictates the level of homogamous choosiness. In both scenarios, one type has an advantage over the other. Assuming an initial proportion b of individuals are of the advantaged type, we give an explicit formula for the asymptotic proportion of the population's genome that originates from these advantaged ancestors under an infinite population size approximation. Our results enable a comparison of the relative strengths of homogamous choosiness, attractiveness, and viability selection in terms of genome transmission, and prove notably that viability selection is always more efficient than both forms of reproductive selection.
item.dc:creator: Juan Mardomingo-Sanz (SIMBA, IECL), Rapha\"el Tran-Thanh (LTCI, IP Paris), Camille Coron (MIA Paris-Saclay, INRAE), Diala Abu Awad (GQE-Le Moulon, INRAE)

item.title: Spatial structure promotes coexistence, resilience, and synergy in microbial communities
item.description: arXiv:2611.00222v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Microbial communities are highly complex systems with a tremendous number of interactions. They thrive in vastly different environments, from the human body to soil and marine ecosystems, and show remarkable properties such as coexistence, diversity, and resilience. Additionally, they are almost always spatially structured. However, the role of space in shaping microbial communities remains poorly understood, in part because explicitly modeling space substantially increases model complexity and limits further exploration of its effects across different settings. Here, we present a minimal theoretical model that incorporates spatial structure into a consumer-resource framework through local and global nutrient consumption. Using this model, we explore the effect of spatial structure on several important properties of microbial communities. We find that spatial structure promotes coexistence under nutrient limitation, increases community resilience to environmental fluctuations, and allows communities to benefit synergistically from poor nutrients. We then extend the model to make spatial structure adaptive, allowing species to become more isolated when competition threatens their presence. Our results show that moderate spatial adaptation promotes coexistence, while weak and strong adaptation do not. Interestingly, strong spatial adaptation can substantially increase community coexistence under environmental fluctuations, while not necessarily promoting coexistence in the absence of fluctuations. Together, our results provide a simple framework for exploring how spatial structure shapes microbial community assembly, dynamics, and response to fluctuating environments.
item.dc:creator: Motasem ElGamel, Andrew Mugler

item.title: Sharp transitions between optimal therapy regimes reveal robust dosing strategies against drug-induced persistence
item.description: arXiv:2611.00295v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Anti-cancer drug treatment can induce tumor cells to adopt reversible drug-tolerant persister states, facilitating resistance evolution and eventual treatment failure. Although low-dose and intermittent therapies have been proposed as alternatives to maximum tolerated dose (MTD) therapy in this setting, it remains unclear when and why these strategies are optimal. To address this question, we develop a mathematical model of drug-induced persistence where the drug can promote switching to a drug-tolerant state or inhibit reversions to sensitivity in a dose-dependent manner. We uncover sharp transitions between qualitatively distinct therapy regimes, including intermittent high-dose and continuous low-dose therapy, driven by the relative dose sensitivities of cell death and phenotypic switching. In particular, intermittent treatment is optimal when the drug inhibits reversions at doses too low to effectively kill the sensitive cells. We finally exploit the simple regime structure of optimal therapies to show that robust alternatives to MTD therapy can be identified under incomplete knowledge of the underlying dynamics
item.dc:creator: Einar Bjarki Gunnarsson

item.title: A resident-traveller model for global aspects of vaccination
item.description: arXiv:2611.01555v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A model for the spread of a vaccine-preventable infectious disease is set in a resident-traveller metapopulation context to investigate global aspects of vaccination. Of particular interest here is the effect of varying vaccine coverage in some patches on the spread of disease in the whole system. Analytically and numerically, the resident-traveller framework is compared with a classic metapopulation model where individuals become residents of the patch they move to. A numerical example inspired by the 2003--2004 poliomyelitis resurgence in western and central Africa is then considered, illustrating how heterogeneous vaccine coverage can sustain widespread regional transmission that classic metapopulation models predict to be much smaller.
item.dc:creator: Julien Arino, P. van den Driessche

item.title: Keep on growing or change direction? Dependence of clonal plant survival on the probability of side-branching
item.description: arXiv:2611.02700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In clonal organisms, the genetic individual (genet) may consist of several physiological individuals (ramets). Clonal plants typically grow horizontally by means of stolons or other clonal growth organs. Some species grow linearly for several ramet generations, while others produce side branches frequently. We hypothesize that the probability of side-branching ($b$) affects genet survival ($G$) depending on the ramets' ratio of birth to death rates ($\lambda$). We used a spatially explicit model of ramet population dynamics to compare three growth strategies. In the neutral case, growing forward and side-branching were equally probable, whereas forward-growing and side-branching plants had lower and higher $b$, respectively. We found that the genet's survival threshold (the critical $\lambda_c$) strongly depended on the branching probability. The lowest threshold, and hence the broadest range of survival, occurred in moderately forward-growing plants, in which the average length of linear (non-branching) intervals was $1.89$ units. Above the threshold, the $G(b)$ relationship strongly depended on $\lambda$. Genet survival was promoted by forward growth in sparse ramet populations (low $\lambda$). However, this advantage gradually disappeared as $\lambda$ increased, and branching probability became effectively neutral across a broad parameter range encompassing both forward-growing and side-branching plants. This suggests strong selection for low branching intensity in unfavorable habitats, but weak or negligible selection in favorable habitats.
item.dc:creator: R\'obert Juh\'asz, Be\'ata Oborny

item.title: Identifying unknown time delay and spatially varying coefficients in a reaction-diffusion equation from boundary measurements
item.description: arXiv:2609.10222v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This work investigates an inverse problem for a general class of linear reaction-diffusion systems incorporating multiple delayed contributions, namely retarded diffusion, retarded time derivatives, and retarded source terms. The objective is to simultaneously recover the unknown time lag $\tau>0$ and spatially heterogeneous coefficients from boundary flux measurements alone. The recovery strategy exploits the singular temporal behavior generated by an incompatibility between the prescribed initial history and the boundary data. In contrast to prior inverse problems for delay equations, which assume $\tau$ known and are confined to ODE or abstract settings, our approach operates in a parabolic PDE framework with spatially varying coefficients. Once $\tau$ is identified, we establish a Lipschitz stability estimate via a Carleman inequality, in the case of time-independent coefficients $p=p(x)$, $q=q(x)$. This is the first result to simultaneously recover an unknown delay and spatially dependent coefficients in a delayed parabolic PDE from boundary data.
item.dc:creator: Ming-Hui Ding, Hongyu Liu, Catharine W. K. Lo

item.title: Evolutionary characterization of whole-genome doubling across human cancers
item.description: arXiv:2611.01897v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Whole-genome doubling (WGD) is common across human cancers and is associated with tumour progression and adverse clinical outcomes. However, how genome-doubled tumours evolve across diverse cancer types remains poorly understood. Here we characterize WGD-associated tumour evolution by integrating genomic analyses of 41,332 tumours from 12 cancer types with evolutionary timing and multi-omic data. Several canonical driver mutations generally preceded WGD when both occurred, as did the onset of homologous recombination deficiency-associated mutagenesis. Notably, post-WGD chromosome-arm losses showed substantially weaker cancer-type dependence than pre-WGD losses, with 61-75% less variance explained by cancer type. Beyond chromosomal evolution, WGD+ tumours showed reduced interferon-response and HLA antigen-presentation programmes linked to epigenetic remodelling, without disproportionate enrichment of genetic immune-escape alterations. Our findings highlight WGD as a recurrent evolutionary transition associated with altered chromosomal evolution and epigenetically linked immune adaptation across cancers.
item.dc:creator: Yangyang Zhang, Haiming Li, Xiaoyu Zhao, Zilong Wang, Yongqi Chen, Sumeng Yang, Shaocong Mo, Jinming Li, Xiaohua Wu, Xu Wang, Shuo Wang, Qinhao Guo

item.title: Can AI Do Formal Demography? Why Vaccinating the Oldest Saves Both the Most Lives and the Most Years of Life
item.description: arXiv:2611.03500v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Can AI contribute to formal demography? We report an experiment in which an AI model, Claude, was asked to explain and then simplify the proof of an earlier result: that vaccinating the oldest against COVID-19 saves both the most lives and the most years of life, because the years saved per person treated rise with age. The model proposed a new proof that is shorter, more intuitive, and somewhat more general than the original, built from a known life-table identity and the definition of convexity. It states the condition for the result as the convexity of the reciprocal of the hazard, which can be checked from the hazard alone and holds for most familiar parametric models, and it yields a lower bound on life expectancy whenever that condition is met. Prompted by a further question, the model also gave an exact form of the condition, showing how far convexity can be relaxed. The model traced these identities and related results in earlier literature. An edited record of the sessions is provided, and complete transcripts are available on request. The exercise suggests that AI can revisit established results, make them easier to understand, and prove valuable generalizations.
item.dc:creator: Joshua R. Goldstein, Kenneth W. Wachter

item.title: A phenotype-structured reaction-diffusion model of avascular glioma growth
item.description: arXiv:2509.22519v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider a phenotype-structured reaction-diffusion model of avascular glioma growth. The model describes the interaction dynamics between tumour cells and oxygen, and takes into account anisotropic cell movement and oxygen diffusion related to structural anisotropy of the brain's extracellular environment. In this model, phenotypic heterogeneity of tumour cells is captured by a continuous phenotype-structuring variable, the value of which evolves due to phenotypic changes. We first analyse a one-dimensional version of the model and formally show, through a Hopf-Cole transformation, that it admits, in appropriate asymptotic regimes, phenotypically heterogeneous travelling wave solutions, wherein the locally prevailing cell phenotype varies across the wave due to the presence of oxygen gradients. This provides a mathematical formalisation for the emergence of intratumour phenotypic heterogeneity driven by differences in oxygen availability across the tumour. We then report on the results of both 1D simulations, which corroborate the results of formal asymptotic analyses, and 2D simulations, which also demonstrate the impact of anisotropy in cell movement and oxygen diffusion on tumour growth and on the phenotypic composition of the tumour edge. These results are complemented with additional results of 3D simulations, which are carried out on the geometry of the brain by using a hybrid finite difference-finite element method and integrating patient-specific magnetic resonance imaging data with diffusion tensor imaging data.
item.dc:creator: Francesca Ballatore, Xinran Ruan, Chiara Giverso, Tommaso Lorenzi

item.title: Behavioral patterns and mean-field games in epidemiological models
item.description: arXiv:2512.20547v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce a new type of Mean Field Game epidemiological models, in which subpopulations have different behavioral patterns: some people exhibit a type of ``rational'' self interested behavior by choosing Nash-equilibrium long-term strategies while others follow pre-specified ``non-rational'' patterns (e.g., either sticking to their usual habits or trying to mimic those around them). Our new B-MFG models allow for occasional behavioral switches, which rational individuals also take into account when formulating their Nash-equilibrium strategies. Although this modeling approach is general, here we develop it for individuals choosing their ``contact rates'' within a particular Susceptible-Infected-Recovered-Susceptible-Dead (SIRSD) epidemic model. The latter is based on a frequency-based force of infection with proportionate mixing and the mortality rate that rapidly increases once the proportion of infected individuals exceeds some prescribed threshold, resulting in a strain on medical resources. Numerical tests illustrate the properties of our model and highlight the ways in which additional/non-rational behavioral patterns and behavioral switching increase the impact of infectious diseases. The paper aims to build a bridge between two distinct communities of epidemiological modelers and to promote the consideration of behavioral patterns in broader Mean Field Games literature.
item.dc:creator: Finnegan Buckley, Alexander Vladimirsky

item.title: A stochastic epidemic model with memory of the last infection and waning immunity
item.description: arXiv:2505.00601v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We adapt the article of Forien, Pang, Pardoux and Zotsa, on epidemic models with varying infectivity and waning immunity, to incorporate the memory of the last infection. To this end, we introduce a parametric approach and consider a piecewise deterministic Markov process modeling both the evolution of the parameter, also called the trait, and the age of infection of individuals over time. At each new infection, a new trait is randomly chosen for the infected individual according to a Markov kernel, and their age is reset to zero. In the large population limit, we derive a partial differential equation (PDE) that describes the density of traits and ages. The main goal is to study the conditions under which endemic equilibria exist for the deterministic PDE model and to establish an endemicity threshold that depends on the model parameters. The local stability of these equilibria is also analyzed. The endemicity threshold is computed for several examples, including models that incorporate a vaccination policy, and a local stability result is obtained for a memory-free SIS-type model.
item.dc:creator: H\'el\`ene Gu\'erin, Arsene Brice Zotsa-Ngoufack

item.title: How Withheld Punishment Sustains Anti-Democratic Behavior in an Evolutionary Game
item.description: arXiv:2512.06245v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Democratic backsliding is often framed as a contest between defenders and disruptors of democratic institutions. That framing can miss a third response, withholding punishment from disruptors while penalizing defenders who confront them. We model the three responses as strategies in an evolutionary game, track their shares with replicator dynamics, and assume defenders beat disruptors head-to-head but have a payoff disadvantage among non-punishers even when disruptors are absent. If the third response cannot spread among disruptors, a payoff condition draws the population toward the classical May--Leonard heteroclinic cycle, a rock--paper--scissors succession in which disruption repeatedly becomes rare, then widespread. If that response can, a threshold on its payoff advantage over disruptors determines whether all three coexist or defenders alone vanish. In finite-population simulations, sustained resurgence requires reintroducing lost strategies. Our contribution is to show how two separately documented political tendencies, if combined, can sustain disruption despite defenders' head-to-head advantage over disruptors.
item.dc:creator: Chad M. Topaz

item.title: Logarithmic scaling of selective sweep curves: from tents to houses
item.description: arXiv:2605.10617v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: One of the classical results of mathematical population genetics states that the frequency of a beneficial mutant's offspring, on its way to fixation in a large population, looks like a logistic curve. A logarithmic scaling (both in height and time) of these selective sweep curves leads (in the case of strong selection) to a tent-like shape in the large population limit: First the logarithmic frequency of the mutant increases linearly from 0 to 1, then that of the former resident decreases from 1 to 0. For moderate selection the logarithmic frequencies develop (in the large population limit) a jump at the beginning/the end of the sweep, which takes the shape of the tent into that of a house. Our main result (proved for the Moran model) assesses the regularity of this convergence in the large population limit: It is uniform in the house's roof (phases of linear growth and decline) and "Skorokhod $M_1$" in the house's walls (closely around the jumps). Apart from interest in its own right, we anticipate that this result and the proof techniques will be instrumental for extending the description of clonal interference by Poissonian interacting trajectories (as it was done in Hermann et al. (2024) for strong selection) also to moderate selection.
item.dc:creator: Florin Boenkost, Felix Hermann, Andr\'as T\'obi\'as, Anton Wakolbinger

item.title: Oxygenation and spatial heterogeneity shape radiotherapy protocol ranking through phenotypic adaptation
item.description: arXiv:2606.04004v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tumor response to radiotherapy is strongly influenced by oxygen availability and phenotypic heterogeneity, yet their combined impact on the relative performance of fractionation schedules remains unclear. Here, we develop a mathematical model that integrates spatial oxygen dynamics with continuous phenotypic adaptation to hypoxia and radiation, and use it to systematically compare radiotherapy protocols under a common normal-tissue toxicity constraint. Under spatially uniform oxygenation, we find that alternative fractionation schedules provide little improvement over standard-of-care protocols in normoxic conditions. Under moderate hypoxia, however, a distinct class of protracted schedules with longer inter-fraction intervals substantially increases time-to-progression, in some cases by up to twofold. This regime-dependent benefit is consistent with a shift in the balance between reoxygenation and selection for resistant phenotypes. When oxygen delivery is spatially heterogeneous, treatment outcomes depend strongly on the geometric organization of oxygen sources. Even with identical total oxygen supply, different spatial configurations lead to large variability in time-to-progression and can alter the relative ranking of radiotherapy protocols. These results show that radiotherapy effectiveness is not an intrinsic property of a treatment schedule alone, but emerges from its interaction with tumor microenvironmental structure and evolutionary dynamics. Incorporating both spatial heterogeneity and phenotypic adaptation may therefore be important for the consistent evaluation and design of fractionation strategies in heterogeneous tumors.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Albanese, Giulia Chiari, Marcello Edoardo Delitala

item.title: Hybrid epidemic simulation framework coupling equation-based and individual-based models
item.description: arXiv:2609.35162v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Mass gathering events (MGEs) can create intense, short-lived transmission hotspots whose effects propagate through urban populations. Quantifying these effects requires linking fine-scale interactions during gatherings with epidemic transmission across metropolitan mobility networks. We developed a hybrid multiscale simulation framework coupling empirically derived individual-based contact networks for MGEs with a stochastic metapopulation susceptible-exposed-infected-recovered (SEIR) model. Using population and commuting data from Madrid, Spain, we investigated how event-related transmission affects epidemic dynamics and district-level invasion. Across the scenarios examined, MGEs increased epidemic peak incidence and accelerated epidemic progression, although the magnitude of these effects depended on event-specific contact patterns and background transmissibility. Dense contact patterns produced greater epidemic amplification, whereas measures reducing close-contact interactions weakened these effects. MGEs also advanced epidemic invasion across districts and increased the temporal synchronization of arrival times, producing a more synchronized metropolitan epidemic wave. The association between MGEs and earlier district-level invasion was partly explained by the size of the event-generated epidemic seed. The main patterns persisted across the epidemiological parameter ranges examined. The framework provides a multiscale approach for investigating how mass gathering management may influence metropolitan epidemic dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Jaeyoung Kwak, Michael H. Lees, Chin Chun Ooi, Wentong Cai

item.title: A five-species counterexample to the Hofbauer--Kon--Saito conjecture on qualitative permanence
item.description: arXiv:2610.38374v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hofbauer, Kon and Saito showed that a Lotka-Volterra interaction matrix $A$ with negative diagonal can be qualitatively permanent only if (C1) every cycle of length $\ge 2$ of $A$ is nonpositive and (C2) every negative cycle contains exactly one negative entry. They conjectured that these conditions are also sufficient, and proved this for $n\le 3$. We give a $5\times 5$ integer matrix with seven nonzero off-diagonal entries that satisfies (C1) and (C2) but is not qualitatively permanent. For an explicit integer growth vector, in which one species is an obligate consumer as the definition allows, the system has an interior equilibrium, and an asymptotically stable heteroclinic cycle on the boundary of the orthant attracts an open set of interior orbits. Adding non-interacting species gives counterexamples for every $n\ge 5$. The interactions form a one-way feedback loop together with a predator of two prey. The verification is elementary except for one heteroclinic connection, which lies in a face that is not Volterra-Lyapunov stable. For it we prove a connection lemma based on invasion graphs, which reduces the question to a smaller, stable face. The failure is robust. It persists under small perturbations, including weak additional interactions, so every sign pattern that satisfies (C1) and (C2) and contains ours is a counterexample, and it occurs for an open cone of growth vectors. For $n\ge 6$ there are also counterexamples in which every species grows when alone. Finally, we announce that the conjecture holds for $n=4$ and that, for $n=5$, four minimal sign patterns characterise its failure.
item.dc:creator: Beldiman Miruna-Mihaela, Halanay Andrei-Dan
